topic.title: a.c. and d.c., switching, plugs, fuses, earthing and double insulation
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: P2 sets this topic every year as short parts worth 1 to 6 marks: a.c. and d.c. [3] with a CRO sketch [1] (Summer 2025), the plug [4]–[6] (Summer 2019, 2023, 2026), the fuse [3] and double insulation [2] (Summer 2024), and the current from P = I × V with the fuse chosen [3]–[4] (Summer 2019, 2023), often in a chain after the heating effect.
mustMemorise: d.c. flows in one direction only (cells, batteries); a.c. changes direction regularly (the mains)
On a CRO: d.c. is a flat line on one side of zero; a.c. is a wave crossing the zero line
Live: brown, through the fuse, brings the supply. Neutral: blue, completes the circuit. Earth: green and yellow, to a metal case
The switch and the fuse always go in the live wire
Fault: live touches the metal case, a large current flows to earth, the fuse melts, the circuit is broken
Double insulated: plastic case, no earth wire, the double-square symbol
Fuse: I = P ÷ V, then the smallest of 3 A, 5 A and 13 A above the current
notOnThisSpec: Circuit breakers and residual current devices
The voltages of the live, neutral and earth wires as numbers

note.title: a.c. and d.c., switching, plugs, fuses, earthing and double insulation
note.subject: science

mustKnow: P = I × V, turned round as I = P ÷ V
Fuse ratings: 3 A, 5 A, 13 A; choose the smallest above the normal current

mustBeAbleTo: Describe the difference between a.c. and d.c., and give a source of each
Recognise, and pick out, the CRO traces of a.c. and d.c.
Explain why the switch (and the fuse) is always in the live wire
Name each wire in a three-pin plug with its colour, its pin and its job
Explain how the earth wire and the fuse together protect the user when the live wire touches a metal case
Describe fully how a fuse protects: current too high, fuse melts, circuit broken
Explain double insulation: a plastic case that cannot become live, so no earth wire
Calculate a current from I = P ÷ V (kilowatts converted first) and choose the fuse: 3 A, 5 A or 13 A
sheet.howExamined: P2 (1 hour 15 minutes, calculator allowed) sets this topic as short parts, usually 1 to 6 marks each: a.c. and d.c. described and the d.c. trace sketched on a CRO grid; the plug's wires named or coloured in boxes; how the fuse protects, as a description or a sentence to complete; double insulation as a tick box and a reason; and the current from P = I × V with the fuse to fit, often straight after the heating effect.
traps: Describing a.c. without saying it changes direction regularly, or d.c. without 'one direction' (Summer 2025 P2 F Q7)
Sketching the a.c. wave when the CRO question asks for d.c. (Summer 2025 P2 F Q7; Summer 2025 P2 H Q3)
Writing only 'the fuse melts': the marks also need the current becoming too high and the circuit being broken (Summer 2024 P2 F Q6; Summer 2024 P2 H Q3)
Saying double insulation is two layers of insulation on the wires, instead of no earth wire and a case that cannot become live (Summer 2024 P2 F Q6; Summer 2024 P2 H Q3)
Not seeing that the fuse melts because the excessive current heats it (Summer 2023 P2 F Q6; Summer 2023 P2 H Q1)
Leaving the power in kilowatts in I = P ÷ V (Summer 2023 P2 F Q6; Summer 2023 P2 H Q1; Summer 2025 P2 H Q5)
Misremembering P = I × V, or turning it round the wrong way, before choosing a fuse (Summer 2025 P2 F Q7)

noteBlocks.lede: Mains electricity reaches your home as a.c. at 230 V, far more than any battery. Every safety feature in a plug keeps the live wire away from you. You will learn the three wires, the switch, the fuse, the earth wire and double insulation, and how to choose the right fuse.
can: Describe a.c. and d.c., and pick out their traces on a CRO
Explain how the fuse, the earth wire and double insulation protect you
Calculate an appliance's current and choose its fuse: 3 A, 5 A or 13 A

noteBlocks.md: A kettle, a heater and a phone charger all plug into the same socket. Behind the wall, the mains supply pushes a current round each of them at 230 volts, enough to kill.

noteBlocks.caption: The live wire brings the supply through the fuse and switch; the neutral returns it; the earth wire guards the metal case.

noteBlocks.md: An appliance joins the mains by two wires. The **live** wire brings the supply in and the **neutral** wire completes the circuit back. The live wire is the dangerous one: touch it and a current can pass through you to the ground. The **earth** wire carries no current at all in normal use. It is a safety route, joined to a metal case.

noteBlocks.prompt: In an appliance's mains circuit, which wire brings the supply in and is dangerous to touch?
options: the live wire
the neutral wire
the earth wire
noteBlocks.explain: Follow the circuit from the supply: the live wire brings the supply in, through the fuse and the switch, and the neutral wire carries it back. The earth wire carries nothing in normal use; it is only a safety route. The dangerous one is the live wire.

noteBlocks.caption: The same oscilloscope, two supplies: d.c. stays on one side of zero; a.c. crosses zero again and again.

noteBlocks.md: A cell or battery gives **direct current (d.c.)**: it flows in **one direction only**. On an oscilloscope (a **CRO**) that is a flat line on one side of the zero line. The mains gives **alternating current (a.c.)**: it **changes direction**, over and over, **regularly**. On the CRO that is a wave rising above the zero line and falling below it.
One full rise and fall is one cycle. The UK mains goes through 50 cycles every second: its frequency is 50 hertz.

noteBlocks.prompt: On a CRO screen with a zero line across the middle, which trace shows alternating current?
options: a wave that crosses the zero line
a flat line above the zero line
a wave that stays above the zero line
noteBlocks.answer: a wave that crosses the zero line
noteBlocks.explain: Alternating current changes direction, and on a CRO a change of direction means the trace crosses the zero line, as the mains wave does. A flat line above zero is a cell's d.c., and a wave that never crosses zero never changes direction. The answer is the wave that crosses the zero line.

noteBlocks.md: The video is made for another exam board: its 'potential difference' is what CCEA calls voltage, and anything about peak voltage or the National Grid is not on the CCEA specification.

A full answer, line by line:
**d.c.** Flows in one direction only. Source: a cell or battery.
**a.c.** Changes direction, and does so regularly. Source: the mains.
**Sketch for d.c.** A flat line on one side of zero, never the wave.

noteBlocks.md: A switch makes or breaks the circuit: on, its two terminals are joined; off, the gap stops the current. It always goes in the **live** wire, because switching off should cut the appliance off from the supply. A switch in the neutral wire stops the current too, but it leaves everything inside **still joined to the live wire**, so touching the appliance could still give a shock.

noteBlocks.prompt: A lamp's switch has been fitted in the neutral wire and is turned off. Why is this dangerous?
options: the lamp is still joined to the live wire
the lamp stays switched on
the current through the lamp becomes too high
noteBlocks.answer: the lamp is still joined to the live wire
noteBlocks.explain: Look at the lower circuit: with the switch off in the neutral wire, the lamp goes dark, but the thick line shows it is still joined to the live wire. Touching the lamp's insides could give a shock. That is why the switch belongs in the live wire. The answer is that the lamp is still joined to the live wire.

noteBlocks.md:
Each wire in a plug has its own colour, pin and job:
**Live.** Brown, to the bottom right, through the fuse. It brings the supply in.
**Neutral.** Blue, to the bottom left. It completes the circuit.
**Earth.** Green and yellow, to the top pin. A safety wire, joined to a metal case.
The **cable grip** clamps the cable so no wire can be pulled loose.

noteBlocks.prompt: In a three-pin plug, which wire is connected through the fuse?
options: the brown live wire
the blue neutral wire
the green and yellow earth wire
noteBlocks.explain: In the plug the fuse sits between the bottom-right terminal and its pin, and the brown live wire goes there. The fuse must be in the wire that brings the supply in, so that melting cuts the supply off. The answer is the brown live wire.

noteBlocks.md: A **fuse** is a thin wire in the live side that melts if the current through it is too big. Suppose a loose live wire touches a metal case. With no earth wire, the case would be live, and touching it could kill. With the earth wire, a **very large current** flows from the live wire, through the case, down to earth.

noteBlocks.md:
In order:
**1.** The live wire touches the metal case.
**2.** A very large current flows through the case and the earth wire.
**3.** The current heats the fuse wire, and it melts.
**4.** The circuit is broken: the live supply is cut off, so the case is safe.

noteBlocks.prompt: When the live wire touches an earthed metal case, what makes the fuse melt?
options: a very large current heats the fuse wire
the case's voltage rises above 230 V
the earth wire pushes current back into the fuse
noteBlocks.answer: a very large current heats the fuse wire
noteBlocks.explain: Go back to step 2 and 3: the fault lets a very large current flow down the earth wire, and that current passes through the fuse in the live wire and heats its thin wire until it melts. Summer 2023 examiners found the heating was what most answers missed. The answer is that a very large current heats the fuse wire.

A three-mark 'describe how a fuse protects' question, marked line by line:
**Mark 1.** The current becomes too high.
**Mark 2.** The fuse wire melts.
**Mark 3.** The circuit is broken, so the current stops.

noteBlocks.title: Where the marks went
noteBlocks.md: **Summer 2024:** no question on that paper was answered worse. Most candidates wrote that the fuse melted and stopped there: one mark of three.

noteBlocks.prompt: A three-mark answer on how a fuse protects an appliance says: 'The current becomes too high and the fuse melts.' Which line would earn the missing mark?
options: The circuit is broken, so the current stops.
The fuse absorbs the extra current.
The fuse is in the live wire.
noteBlocks.answer: The circuit is broken, so the current stops.
noteBlocks.explain: The three marks follow the chain: the current becomes too high, the fuse melts, and the melting breaks the circuit so the current stops. The answer has the first two links; the missing one is what melting achieves. A fuse absorbs nothing, and where it sits does not describe what it does. The answer is that the circuit is broken, so the current stops.

noteBlocks.md: Some appliances, like most hairdryers, have a **plastic** case. Plastic is an insulator, so even if a live wire came loose inside, the outside could never become live. There is nothing for an earth wire to protect, so the cable has **no earth wire**: only live and neutral. These appliances are **double insulated** and carry the double-square symbol.
Double insulation does not mean two layers of insulation on the wires. That was the commonest wrong answer in Summer 2024.

noteBlocks.prompt: How many earth wires are in the cable of a double-insulated hairdryer?
options: no earth wire
one earth wire
two earth wires
noteBlocks.explain: An earth wire protects a metal case by giving a fault current a path to earth. A double-insulated hairdryer has a plastic case that can never become live, so there is nothing to protect: its cable has live and neutral only. The answer is no earth wire.

noteBlocks.caption: Work out the normal current, then take the next fuse up: 3.5 A needs a 5 A fuse.

noteBlocks.md: A plug takes a 3 A, 5 A or 13 A fuse: the smallest one **just above** the appliance's normal current. So find the current first, from **P = I × V**, turned round as **I = P ÷ V**.

noteBlocks.title: Why just above the current
noteBlocks.md: Below the normal current, a fuse melts in normal use. Far above it, a fuse may not melt in a fault. The smallest fuse above the current does both jobs.

An 805 W coffee machine:
**Step 1.** P = I × V
**Step 2.** 805 = I × 230
**Step 3.** I = 805 ÷ 230 = 3.5 A
**Step 4.** 3 A is too small, so the fuse is 5 A

noteBlocks.prompt: A food mixer is rated 368 W and runs on the 230 V mains. What is its normal current, in amps?
noteBlocks.explain: Turn P = I × V round, as in the steps: I = P ÷ V = 368 ÷ 230 = 1.6 A. Its fuse would then be 3 A, the smallest above 1.6 A.

noteBlocks.md: Powers are often given in kilowatts. Convert to watts first, or the current comes out 1000 times too small; Summer 2023 examiners saw marks lost exactly there.

noteBlocks.md:
A 2.53 kW kettle on the 230 V mains:
**Convert.** 2.53 kW = 2530 W
**Current.** I = 2530 ÷ 230 = 11 A
**Choose.** 11 A is above 5 A, so the fuse is 13 A

noteBlocks.prompt: A heater is rated 1.38 kW and runs on the 230 V mains. What is its normal current, in amps?
noteBlocks.explain: Convert first, as the kettle did: 1.38 kW = 1380 W. Then I = 1380 ÷ 230 = 6 A. Left in kilowatts, 1.38 ÷ 230 gives a current 1000 times too small. Its fuse would be 13 A.

noteBlocks.md: **Names or colours?** The plug question asks for the wires' names (Summer 2023), their colours (Summer 2026) or both, for [6] (Summer 2019). Read what each box wants before you write.

**The fuse list changes.** Summer 2019 offered 1 A, 3 A and 5 A. Whatever the list, take the smallest fuse above the current. For 2.2 A:
**Too small.** 1 A: it would melt in normal use.
**Chosen.** 3 A: the smallest above 2.2 A.

noteBlocks.prompt: A question offers 1 A, 3 A and 5 A fuses for an appliance whose normal current is 2.2 A. Which fuse should be chosen?
options: 1 A
3 A
5 A
noteBlocks.explain: The rule is the same whatever the list: the smallest fuse above the current. 1 A is below 2.2 A and would melt in normal use; 5 A is bigger than needed. The answer is 3 A.

noteBlocks.md: **'Which two parts protect the user?'** The fuse and the earth wire, working together (Summer 2026).
**The d.c. sketch.** Asked to sketch what a CRO shows for d.c., draw a flat line on one side of zero (Summer 2025). Many drew the a.c. wave.
**A sentence with gaps.** Summer 2021 set how a fuse works as a sentence to complete: the current is too high, the fuse melts, and that leaves a break in the circuit.

noteBlocks.prompt: The top CRO screen is for d.c. from a cell, and its trace is missing. What should be sketched there?
options: a flat line above the zero line
a wave that crosses the zero line
a flat line along the zero line
noteBlocks.answer: a flat line above the zero line
noteBlocks.explain: Direct current flows one way and stays steady, so its trace is a flat line on one side of zero. The wave belongs on the a.c. screen below it, and a line along zero would mean no current at all. The answer is a flat line above the zero line.

noteBlocks.text: Going further: the whole appliance question

noteBlocks.md: The longest P2 questions chain this topic to the heating effect (Summer 2019, Summer 2023). One chain, start to finish:

A 2.07 kW kettle with a metal case:
**Heat.** Free electrons collide with the metal atoms of the element.
**Current.** 2.07 kW = 2070 W, and I = 2070 ÷ 230 = 9 A.
**Fuse.** 9 A is above 5 A, so 13 A.
**Plug.** The fuse sits in the brown live wire, and the metal case needs the green and yellow earth wire.

noteBlocks.prompt: A 2.07 kW kettle has a metal case. Which set of features must its plug and cable have?
options: a 13 A fuse in the live wire, and an earth wire
a 5 A fuse in the live wire, and an earth wire
a 13 A fuse in the live wire, and no earth wire
noteBlocks.answer: a 13 A fuse in the live wire, and an earth wire
noteBlocks.explain: Go through the chain: the current is 9 A, so the fuse is 13 A, because a 5 A fuse would melt in normal use; and a metal case must be earthed. Only a double-insulated appliance goes without an earth wire. The answer is a 13 A fuse in the live wire, and an earth wire.

noteBlocks.text: Where I = P ÷ V comes from

noteBlocks.md: Every fuse answer needs the current, but the equation you remember gives the power. Turning it round is where Summer 2025 answers slipped, so do it once, slowly, and check it with the units.

**Start.** $P = I \times V$
**Divide both sides by V.** $P \div V = I \times V \div V$
**Cancel the Vs.** $I = P \div V$
**Check the units.** watts ÷ volts = amperes, a current.

noteBlocks.prompt: An appliance on the 230 V mains has a power P. Which expression gives the current I it takes?
options: I = P ÷ V
I = V ÷ P
I = P × V
noteBlocks.explain: Start from P = I × V and divide both sides by V: the Vs on the right cancel and leave I = P ÷ V. The check: watts divided by volts gives amperes. V ÷ P is the upside-down slip, and it makes a bigger power give a smaller current. The answer is I = P ÷ V.

Wire a plug: brown live through the fuse, blue neutral, green and yellow earth.

Say why the switch and fuse are live-side, and why double insulation needs no earth.

P2 sets this topic as short parts: a.c. and d.c. in words [3] and a CRO sketch [1], the plug's wire names or colours [3–6], how the fuse protects [3], double insulation [2], and the current with its fuse [3–4], often straight after the heating effect. The first mark for a fuse is 'the current becomes too high'. Stuck? Write live, fuse, melts, circuit broken.

workedExamples.stem:
A hairdryer has a power rating of 1.61 kW and is used on the 230 V mains.
Calculate the current, then choose the fuse: 3 A, 5 A or 13 A. [5]

steps.decision: The equation first: it earns a mark on its own, and it tells you the current is the power divided by the voltage.
The power must be in watts: multiply kilowatts by 1000.

options: P = I × V needs the power in watts, so 1 kW becomes 1000 W
Kilowatts are divided by 1000 to make watts
The mains voltage is given in kilovolts
whyMenu.explain: P = I × V links watts, amps and volts. A kilowatt is 1000 watts, so the power in watts is the number of kilowatts times 1000. Left in kilowatts, the current comes out 1000 times too small.

steps.decision: Divide the power by the voltage.
7 A is above 3 A and 5 A, so the smallest fuse above it is 13 A.

options: The fuse must be just above the normal current, so it lets it through but melts in a fault
The fuse must be as close to the current as possible, above or below
The biggest fuse is always the safest
whyMenu.explain: A fuse below the normal current melts in normal use; one far above may not melt in a fault. The smallest rating above the current does both jobs.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: I = 7 A, so a 13 A fuse

steps.working: A very large current flows from the live wire, through the case, down the earth wire to earth.
steps.decision: Start with the path the fault opens: the earth wire is a very easy route to earth, so the current is very large.

accepted: a large current flows through the case and the earth wire

steps.working: The large current heats the fuse wire and it melts.
steps.decision: The fuse is in the live wire, so the fault current passes through it too.

options: The large current heats the thin fuse wire until it melts
The fuse soaks up the extra current
The earth wire pushes the current back through the fuse
whyMenu.explain: A fuse is a thin wire. A very large current heats it, and it melts: nothing is soaked up. Summer 2023 examiners found the heating the part most answers missed.

steps.working: The circuit is broken, so the live supply is cut off and the case is no longer live.
steps.decision: Finish with what melting achieves: it is this link that protects the user.

accepted: the circuit is broken so the case is no longer live

workedExamples.finalAnswer: A very large current flows to earth, the fuse melts, and the live supply is cut off, so the case is no longer live.

twin.stem: A lamp has a metal base joined to the earth wire. A fault makes the live wire touch the base. What happens to the fuse, and why? [2]

accepted: a very large current flows to earth, so the fuse melts

workedExamples.stem: Explain what is meant by direct current and by alternating current, and give a source of each. [5]

steps.working: Direct current flows in one direction only.
steps.decision: One mark: the direction never changes.
Two marks: that it changes direction, and that it keeps doing so.

options: 'Regularly' is the second mark: the current keeps changing direction, not just once
'Regularly' means the current is steady
'Regularly' is only needed at Higher tier
whyMenu.explain: A current that changed direction once would not be a.c. The mark scheme wants both ideas: it changes direction, and it does so over and over (50 times a second on the mains).

steps.working: A source of d.c.: a cell or battery.
steps.decision: The current from a cell always goes the same way round.

steps.working: A source of a.c.: the mains.
steps.decision: The mains in the home is a.c.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: d.c. flows in one direction only (a cell); a.c. changes direction regularly (the mains).

twin.stem: Explain what is meant by alternating current. [2]

accepted: a current that changes direction regularly

items.stem: Something from the power topic, which this one uses: a current of 2 A flows at 230 V. What is the power, using P = I × V?

options.feedback: P = I × V = 2 × 230 = 460 W. You will turn this equation round to find a current.
That divides the voltage by the current. Power is current times voltage: P = I × V.
That adds them. Power is current multiplied by voltage: P = I × V.
Kilo means a thousand, not a hundred: multiply by 1000.
That divides by 1000. A kilowatt is bigger than a watt, so the number of watts is bigger: multiply by 1000.

items.stem: A lamp is lit in a complete circuit. What happens to the current if a gap is made anywhere in the circuit?
items.skill: Prerequisite: a break stops the current

options.text: the current stops everywhere in the circuit
options.feedback: A current needs a complete loop: one gap anywhere stops it everywhere. A fuse uses exactly this.

options.text: the current stops only after the gap
options.feedback: The current in a series loop is the same all the way round, so a gap anywhere stops it everywhere.

options.text: the current carries on, but more slowly
options.feedback: A gap means no complete loop, so there is no current at all.
That is a.c.: on the mains, 50 times a second.

options.text: it flows in one direction only
options.feedback: That is direct current, from a cell. Alternating current changes direction, regularly.

options.text: it flows only when a switch is on
options.feedback: Every current needs a closed switch. What makes a current alternating is that it changes direction, regularly.

items.stem: In a three-pin plug, which wire is connected through the fuse?

options.feedback: The fuse is in the live wire, so when it melts the live supply is cut off.
The neutral wire completes the circuit. The fuse goes in the brown live wire, the one that brings the supply in.

options.text: the green and yellow earth wire
options.feedback: The earth wire must never be broken: it is the safety path. The fuse goes in the brown live wire.

items.stem: When a fault makes a very large current flow, why does the fuse melt?

options.text: the large current heats the thin fuse wire
options.feedback: The heating is the reason: a thin wire gets very hot when a large current passes through it.

options.text: the fuse is designed to absorb extra current
options.feedback: A fuse absorbs nothing. The large current heats its thin wire until it melts, and the gap stops the current.

options.text: the earth wire sends a signal to the fuse
options.feedback: There is no signal. The fault current passes through the fuse, heats its thin wire and melts it.

items.stem: Why does a double-insulated appliance not need an earth wire?

options.text: its case is plastic, so the outside can never become live
options.feedback: No metal outside, nothing that could become live, so nothing for an earth wire to protect.

options.text: its wires have two layers of insulation
options.feedback: This was the commonest wrong answer in Summer 2024. Double insulation means the case itself is an insulator, so it can never become live.

options.text: it uses a bigger fuse instead
options.feedback: The fuse is chosen from the current, as usual. No earth wire is needed because the plastic case can never become live.

items.stem: An appliance's normal current is 4 A. Which fuse should it have?

options.feedback: A 3 A fuse is below the normal current of 4 A, so it would melt every time the appliance was switched on. Choose the smallest fuse above 4 A: 5 A.
The normal current is 4 A, and 5 A is the smallest fuse above it: it lets that current through but melts if a fault makes the current much bigger.
A 13 A fuse would work, but it is bigger than it needs to be: a fault could push the current well above 4 A without melting it. The smallest fuse above 4 A is 5 A.

items.stem: Why is a light switch fitted in the live wire?

options.text: so that switching off cuts the lamp off from the live supply
options.feedback: With the switch off, nothing beyond it is joined to live, so the lamp is safe to handle.

options.text: because the switch will not work in the neutral wire
options.feedback: A neutral-wire switch would still turn the lamp off. It is not safe, though: the lamp would stay joined to the live wire.

options.text: so that the current through the lamp is smaller
options.feedback: Where the switch sits does not change the current. It sits in the live wire so that switching off cuts the lamp off from the live supply.

hints: Brown to the bottom right, blue to the bottom left, and the striped one to the top.
parts.workedSolution: A, the earth wire, is green and yellow. C, the live wire, is brown. D, the neutral wire, is blue. Red and black are the colours plugs used long ago, before 2004.

context.setting: The two kinds of current, in words

parts.stem:
A torch runs on direct current (d.c.); a toaster runs on alternating current (a.c.).
Explain what is meant by direct current.

accepted: a current that always flows in one direction

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 Foundation: very few answers showed an adequate understanding of d.c. or a.c.

hints: Think of the current from a cell: which way does it go round the circuit, and does that ever change?
parts.workedSolution: Direct current always flows in one direction.

parts.stem: Explain what is meant by alternating current.

accepted: a current that keeps changing direction, regularly
the current reverses direction many times every second

hints: Two ideas: what the current does, and how often it does it.
parts.workedSolution: Alternating current changes direction, and it does so regularly: the mains changes direction 50 times every second.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows four oscilloscope (CRO) screens, A to D. Each dashed line is the zero line.
Which screen shows the direct current from a cell?

options.feedback: A cell's current flows one way and stays steady, so the trace is a flat line on one side of zero.

B crosses the zero line: the current changes direction, so it is a.c. A cell's d.c. is a flat line on one side of zero, screen A. Summer 2025 examiners saw many sketch the a.c. wave when asked for d.c.
C never crosses zero, but it rises and falls. A cell gives a steady current, a flat line: screen A.
D lies on the zero line: no current at all. A cell's current is a flat line above (or below) zero: screen A.

hints: d.c. goes one way and a cell's current is steady.
parts.workedSolution: Screen A: a flat line on one side of the zero line, because a cell's current flows one way and does not change.

parts.stem: Which screen shows alternating current from the mains?

options.feedback: A is a flat line on one side of zero: current in one direction only, d.c. The mains changes direction, so its trace crosses the zero line: screen B.
The wave goes above and below the zero line: the current changes direction, again and again.
C rises and falls but never crosses zero, so the current never changes direction. Alternating current crosses the zero line: screen B.
D is the zero line itself: no current. Alternating current crosses the zero line: screen B.

hints: Alternating current changes direction. What does changing direction look like against the zero line?
parts.workedSolution: Screen B: the trace crosses the zero line, going above and below it, because the current keeps changing direction.

context.setting: A fault in a hairdryer, one step at a time

parts.stem:
A fault develops in a hairdryer.
State what happens to the size of the current.
hints: A fuse only acts when something about the current changes.
parts.workedSolution: The current becomes too high.

parts.stem: State what happens to the thin wire inside the fuse.
hints: A large current heats a thin wire.
parts.workedSolution: It melts: the large current heats the thin wire until it melts (the fuse blows).

parts.stem: State what this does to the circuit.

accepted: it breaks the circuit, so the current stops

scheme.for: breaks the circuit / leaves a gap, so the current stops

hints: Look at the fuse after the fault: what is left between the two ends?
parts.workedSolution: It breaks the circuit: the melted wire leaves a gap, so the current stops.

parts.stem: Explain why the switch for an appliance is always fitted in the live wire and not in the neutral wire.

accepted: so that when it is switched off the appliance is cut off from the live wire, and it is safe to touch
switching off disconnects the appliance from the live supply, so it cannot give a shock

scheme.for: switching off disconnects the appliance from the live (supply)
so it is safe / cannot give an electric shock

hints: With the switch off, which parts of the appliance are still joined to the live wire?
parts.workedSolution: So that switching off disconnects the appliance from the live wire. Then nothing inside it is live, so it is safe to touch and cannot give a shock. A switch in the neutral wire would stop the current but leave the appliance joined to live.

parts.stem:
A television has a power rating of 575 W.
Calculate the current it takes from the 230 V mains.
hints: Write P = I × V first, then put the numbers in.
Divide the power by the voltage to find the current.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides the voltage by the power: P = I × V turned upside down. The current is the power divided by the voltage, 575 ÷ 230 = 2.5 A. A check: a bigger power must mean a bigger current, and 230 ÷ P does the opposite.

parts.stem: Choose the fuse that should be fitted in its plug.

options.feedback: The normal current is 2.5 A, and 3 A is the smallest fuse above it: it lets that current through but melts if a fault makes the current much bigger.
A 5 A fuse would work, but it is bigger than it needs to be: a fault could push the current well above 2.5 A without melting it. The smallest fuse above 2.5 A is 3 A.
A 13 A fuse would work, but it is bigger than it needs to be: a fault could push the current well above 2.5 A without melting it. The smallest fuse above 2.5 A is 3 A.

hints: The smallest fuse above the current you found.
parts.workedSolution: The current is 2.5 A, and the smallest fuse above it is 3 A.

emphasis: fuse action: high current, melts, circuit broken

context.setting: What a fuse does in a fault

parts.stem: A fault develops in a washing machine. Describe, step by step, how its fuse stops the machine being damaged.

accepted: the current becomes too high, so the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, and the current stops
if the current gets too large the fuse blows, which leaves a gap in the circuit so no current flows

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2024: the weakest answered question of that paper; most answers earned only this mark.

scheme.for: the circuit is broken / the current stops flowing (dependent on the fuse melting)

hints: Three links: what the current does, what the fuse does, and what that does to the circuit.
parts.workedSolution: If a fault makes the current too high, the thin fuse wire heats up and melts. That breaks the circuit, so the current stops and the appliance is not damaged.

commonErrors.feedback: True, the fuse melts, but that is one mark of three. Say what makes it melt (the current becomes too high) and what melting does (it breaks the circuit, so the current stops). Summer 2024 examiners found most answers stopped at 'the fuse melted'.

This symbol is printed on a hairdryer.
Name what the symbol means.
hints: Two squares, one inside the other.
parts.workedSolution: The hairdryer is double insulated.

parts.stem: How many earth wires are in the cable of a double-insulated appliance?

options.feedback: Right: the cable has only a live and a neutral wire. With a plastic case there is no metal outside for an earth wire to protect.
An earth wire protects a metal case. A double-insulated appliance has a plastic case, so its cable has no earth wire at all: just live and neutral.
'Double' does not mean two earth wires. The case is plastic, so there is nothing for an earth wire to protect: the cable has no earth wire.

hints: What does an earth wire protect, and does a plastic case need that?
parts.workedSolution: No earth wire: the cable has only the live and neutral wires.

parts.stem: Explain why the hairdryer is still safe to hold if a live wire comes loose inside it.

accepted: its case is plastic, so the live wire can never make the outside of the appliance live
there are no metal parts outside that a live wire could touch

scheme.for: the (outer) case is an insulator / plastic, so a live wire cannot make it live (no metal parts exposed)

hints: Think about what the case is made of.
parts.workedSolution: Its case is made of plastic, an insulator, so even if a live wire came loose inside, the outside of the appliance could never become live.

commonErrors.feedback: Double insulation is not two layers on the wires. It means the case is made of plastic, an insulator, so a loose live wire can never make the outside live, and no earth wire is needed. Summer 2024 examiners saw this 'two layers' answer more than any other.

parts.stem:
A toaster has a metal case, which is joined to the earth wire. A fault makes the live wire touch the case.
Explain how the earth wire and the fuse together protect the user.

accepted: a very large current flows from the live wire through the case and down the earth wire; this large current melts the fuse, which breaks the circuit so the case is no longer live
the current goes to earth through the earth wire, the current is too high so the fuse blows and cuts off the live supply

scheme.for: through the case and the earth wire, to earth
the live supply is cut off / the circuit is broken, so the case is no longer live

hints: Follow the current from the live wire: where can it go once it reaches the case?
Then: what does that current do to the fuse, and what does the fuse do to the live wire?
parts.workedSolution: A very large current flows from the live wire, through the metal case and down the earth wire to earth. This large current heats the fuse wire until it melts, which breaks the circuit and cuts off the live supply, so the case is no longer live and is safe to touch.

context.setting: A fan heater rated in kilowatts

parts.stem:
A fan heater is rated 1.84 kW.
Calculate the current it takes from the 230 V mains.
hints: Write P = I × V first, then put the numbers in.
The power must be in watts before it goes into the equation.

commonErrors.feedback: The power went in as 1.84, still in kilowatts, so the current is 1000 times too small. Convert first: 1.84 kW = 1840 W, then I = 1840 ÷ 230 = 8 A. Summer 2023 examiners saw marks lost to exactly this conversion.

That divides the voltage by the power: P = I × V turned upside down. The current is the power divided by the voltage, 1840 ÷ 230 = 8 A. A check: a bigger power must mean a bigger current, and 230 ÷ P does the opposite.

parts.stem: Choose the fuse that should be fitted in the heater's plug.

options.feedback: A 3 A fuse is below the normal current of 8 A, so it would melt every time the appliance was switched on. Choose the smallest fuse above 8 A: 13 A.
A 5 A fuse is below the normal current of 8 A, so it would melt every time the appliance was switched on. Choose the smallest fuse above 8 A: 13 A.
The normal current is 8 A, and 13 A is the smallest fuse above it: it lets that current through but melts if a fault makes the current much bigger.

hints: The smallest fuse above the current you found.
parts.workedSolution: The current is 8 A; 5 A is too small, so the fuse is 13 A.

context.setting: The 50 Hz on a rating plate

parts.stem:
The rating plate on a drill says 230 V, 50 Hz. The 50 Hz is the frequency of the alternating current supply.
Explain what is meant by alternating current.

accepted: the current changes direction regularly, 50 times every second

hints: What the current does, and how often.
parts.workedSolution: The current changes direction, regularly: on the mains, 50 times every second.

parts.stem: Which laboratory instrument shows an alternating current as a trace on a screen?
hints: It draws the current's pattern as a trace on a screen.
parts.workedSolution: A cathode ray oscilloscope (CRO), which shows the a.c. as a wave crossing the zero line.

emphasis: why the fuse is in the live wire

context.setting: A fuse fitted in the wrong wire

parts.stem:
A heater with an earthed metal case has had its fuse wrongly fitted in the neutral wire. A fault makes the live wire touch the case.
What happens?

options.text: The large current runs from the live wire to earth without passing through the fuse, so the fuse does not melt.
options.feedback: Right. The fault current goes live, case, earth wire: the neutral wire is not on that path, so a fuse in it feels no extra current and the fault is never cut off.

options.text: The fuse melts, so the heater is made safe.
options.feedback: Follow the fault current: from the live wire into the case and down the earth wire. It never reaches the neutral wire, so a fuse there has no reason to melt. That is why the fuse goes in the live wire.

options.text: No current flows, because the fuse is in the neutral wire.
options.feedback: The fault gives the current a new path, from the live wire through the case to earth, and that path does not include the neutral wire. A very large current flows, and the neutral fuse does not melt.

scheme.for: the fault current bypasses the neutral wire, so the fuse does not melt

hints: Trace the current in the fault: live wire, then where?
parts.workedSolution: The fault current flows from the live wire through the case and down the earth wire. The neutral wire is not on that path, so a fuse in it does not melt and the fault is not cut off.

parts.stem: Where should the fuse have been fitted?

options.feedback: Every current into the appliance, including a fault current to earth, passes through the live wire, so a fuse there always melts in a fault and cuts the live supply off.
A fuse in the earth wire would melt and break the safety path, leaving the case live. The fuse goes in the live wire, which every current passes through.

options.text: in the neutral wire, but a bigger one
options.feedback: Size is not the problem: the fault current never reaches the neutral wire. The fuse goes in the live wire.

hints: Which wire does every current into the appliance pass through?
parts.workedSolution: In the live wire: every current into the appliance, normal or fault, passes through it.

context.setting: An iron: why it gets hot, then its current and its fuse

parts.stem:
An iron has a metal heating element. When it is switched on, the element gets hot.
Name the main form of energy produced in the element.
hints: What is the iron for?
parts.workedSolution: Heat (thermal energy).

commonErrors.feedback: Electrical energy is what goes in; the question asks what the element produces. The electrons' collisions make the metal atoms vibrate more: that is heat. Summer 2025 examiners saw many lose this mark to the word electrical.

parts.stem: Describe how the particles in the element produce this energy.

accepted: the free electrons collide with the metal atoms and give them energy, so the atoms vibrate more

hints: Name both particles and say what happens when they meet.
parts.workedSolution: The free electrons carrying the current collide with the metal atoms of the element and give them energy, so the atoms vibrate more and the element heats up.

commonErrors.feedback: The electrons collide with whole metal atoms, held in place in the element, not with particles from inside the nucleus.

parts.stem:
The iron is rated 1.035 kW.
Calculate the current it takes from the 230 V mains.
hints: Write P = I × V first, then put the numbers in.
The power must be in watts before it goes into the equation.

commonErrors.feedback: The power went in as 1.035, still in kilowatts, so the current is 1000 times too small. Convert first: 1.035 kW = 1035 W, then I = 1035 ÷ 230 = 4.5 A. Summer 2023 examiners saw marks lost to exactly this conversion.

That divides the voltage by the power: P = I × V turned upside down. The current is the power divided by the voltage, 1035 ÷ 230 = 4.5 A. A check: a bigger power must mean a bigger current, and 230 ÷ P does the opposite.

parts.stem: Choose the fuse for the iron's plug.

options.feedback: A 3 A fuse is below the normal current of 4.5 A, so it would melt every time the appliance was switched on. Choose the smallest fuse above 4.5 A: 5 A.
The normal current is 4.5 A, and 5 A is the smallest fuse above it: it lets that current through but melts if a fault makes the current much bigger.
A 13 A fuse would work, but it is bigger than it needs to be: a fault could push the current well above 4.5 A without melting it. The smallest fuse above 4.5 A is 5 A.

hints: The smallest fuse above the current you found.
parts.workedSolution: The current is 4.5 A; 3 A is too small and 5 A is the next one up, so the fuse is 5 A.

parts.stem:
A kettle has a power rating of 2.185 kW.
Calculate the current it takes from the 230 V mains.
hints: Write P = I × V first, then put the numbers in.
The power must be in watts before it goes into the equation.

commonErrors.feedback: The power went in as 2.185, still in kilowatts, so the current is 1000 times too small. Convert first: 2.185 kW = 2185 W, then I = 2185 ÷ 230 = 9.5 A. Summer 2023 examiners saw marks lost to exactly this conversion.

That divides the voltage by the power: P = I × V turned upside down. The current is the power divided by the voltage, 2185 ÷ 230 = 9.5 A. A check: a bigger power must mean a bigger current, and 230 ÷ P does the opposite.

parts.stem: Choose the fuse that should be fitted in the kettle's plug.

options.feedback: A 3 A fuse is below the normal current of 9.5 A, so it would melt every time the appliance was switched on. Choose the smallest fuse above 9.5 A: 13 A.
A 5 A fuse is below the normal current of 9.5 A, so it would melt every time the appliance was switched on. Choose the smallest fuse above 9.5 A: 13 A.
The normal current is 9.5 A, and 13 A is the smallest fuse above it: it lets that current through but melts if a fault makes the current much bigger.

hints: The smallest fuse above your current.
parts.workedSolution: The current is 9.5 A, so the fuse is 13 A.

parts.stem: Explain why a 5 A fuse would not be suitable for the kettle.

accepted: the normal current is bigger than 5 A, so a 5 A fuse would melt every time the kettle was used

scheme.for: the normal current is above 5 A, so it would melt (blow) in normal use

hints: Compare 5 A with the current you calculated.
parts.workedSolution: The kettle's normal current is 9.5 A, more than 5 A, so a 5 A fuse would melt every time the kettle was switched on.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows the kettle's plug with its back removed.
Choose the name of the wire at A, at C and at D.
hints: Top pin, bottom right through the fuse, bottom left.
parts.workedSolution: A is the earth wire, C is the live wire (through the fuse) and D is the neutral wire.

parts.stem: State what could cause the fuse to melt.

accepted: a current that is too high, for example when a fault joins the live wire to the case

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2023: the main slip was not linking the melting to the heating by a very large current.

hints: What heats the thin fuse wire enough to melt it?
parts.workedSolution: A current that is too high, for example when a fault lets the live wire touch the metal case: the large current heats the fuse wire until it melts.

parts.stem:
Appliances in the home run on two kinds of current: direct current (d.c.) and alternating current (a.c.).
Explain what is meant by direct current.

accepted: a current that flows in one direction only

hints: Which way does a cell's current go, and does it ever change?
parts.workedSolution: Direct current flows in one direction only.

parts.stem: Explain what is meant by alternating current.

accepted: a current that changes direction repeatedly

hints: What it does and how often.
parts.workedSolution: Alternating current changes direction, over and over again: repeatedly, 50 times a second on the mains.

parts.stem:
Name a supply of each kind.
A supply of d.c.
hints: What powers a remote control?
parts.workedSolution: A battery: its current always flows the same way round the circuit.

parts.stem: A supply of a.c.
hints: Where does a kettle get its electricity?
parts.workedSolution: The mains supply.

parts.stem: A CRO is connected to a direct current supply. Which screen, A to D, shows what you would see?

options.feedback: A steady current in one direction: a flat line on one side of the zero line.
B crosses zero, so the current changes direction: that is a.c. The d.c. trace is a flat line on one side of zero, screen A. In Summer 2025 many drew exactly this wave for d.c.
C varies up and down. A d.c. supply gives a steady flat line on one side of zero: screen A.
D is the zero line: no current. A d.c. supply's trace sits above (or below) zero: screen A.

scheme.for: a horizontal line above (or below) the zero line

hints: One direction, steady.
parts.workedSolution: Screen A: a horizontal line on one side of the zero line.

parts.stem: In a fault, how does a fuse keep an appliance from being damaged? Describe it fully.

accepted: the current gets too high, the fuse melts, and the circuit is broken so the current stops

scheme.for: circuit is broken / current stops (dependent on the threshold mark)

hints: Three links: current, fuse, circuit.
parts.workedSolution: The current gets too high, so the fuse wire melts. The circuit is broken and the current stops, so the appliance is protected.

commonErrors.feedback: True, the fuse melts, but that is one mark of three. Say what makes it melt (the current becomes too high) and what melting does (it breaks the circuit, so the current stops). Summer 2024 examiners found most answers stopped at 'the fuse melted'.

parts.stem:
The symbol shown is printed on a vacuum cleaner: it is double insulated.
How many earth wires does the vacuum cleaner's cable have?

options.feedback: A double-insulated appliance has no metal case to protect, so it has no earth wire.
Right: live and neutral only.
'Double' refers to the insulation, not to the earth wire. There is no earth wire at all.

hints: What would an earth wire be joined to?
parts.workedSolution: No earth wire.

parts.stem: Explain why the vacuum cleaner is safe to touch even if a live wire works loose inside it.

accepted: the live wire cannot touch any metal on the outside, because the case is plastic

scheme.for: the case is an insulator with no metal exposed, so a loose live wire cannot make it live

hints: What is the outside made of?
parts.workedSolution: Its case is plastic and has no metal showing, so a loose live wire can never make the outside live.

commonErrors.feedback: Double insulation is not two layers on the wires. It means the case is made of plastic, an insulator, so a loose live wire can never make the outside live, and no earth wire is needed. Summer 2024 examiners saw this 'two layers' answer more than any other.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows a three-pin plug with its back removed.
Choose the colour of the wire at A, at C and at D.
hints: Brown to the bottom right through the fuse, blue to the bottom left.
parts.workedSolution: A (earth) is green and yellow, C (live) is brown, D (neutral) is blue.

parts.stem: Name the two safety parts that act together in a fault to protect the person using the appliance.

accepted: the fuse and the earth wire

hints: One melts; the other carries a fault current away.
parts.workedSolution: The fuse and the earth wire: in a fault the earth wire carries a large current, which melts the fuse and cuts off the live supply.

findTheMistake.stem:
Orla is asked: 'A heater is rated 2.3 kW and runs on the 230 V mains. Calculate the current, and choose the fuse. [5]'
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 puts the power in as 2.3, still in kilowatts. The equation needs watts: 2.3 kW = 2300 W. With kilowatts the current comes out 1000 times too small, and the fuse chosen from it is far too small: it would melt the moment the heater was switched on.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of five, for the equation. A heater drawing a hundredth of an amp could not warm anything, which is the check that catches this. Summer 2023 examiners saw marks lost by not converting kilowatts to watts.

findTheMistake.stem:
Dáire is asked: 'A microwave oven is rated 920 W. Calculate the current it takes from the 230 V mains. [3]'
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 turns P = I × V round the wrong way. Dividing both sides by V gives I = P ÷ V, the power divided by the voltage: 920 ÷ 230 = 4 A, not 230 ÷ 920.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of three, for the equation. Summer 2025 examiners found P = I × V not well recalled by most Foundation candidates, and rearranging it is where it slips. A check: a bigger power should mean a bigger current, and 230 ÷ P does the opposite.

findTheMistake.stem:
Callum is asked: 'A slow cooker is rated 1.265 kW. Calculate its current on the 230 V mains and choose its fuse. [5]'
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 multiplies by 100. Kilo means a thousand: 1.265 kW = 1265 W. Every line after it carries the slip, so the current is ten times too small and the fuse is far too small.
findTheMistake.feedback: The conversion mark is lost and the current and fuse follow from it. Summer 2025 Higher examiners noted that the kilo prefix proved a problem for some candidates. One kilowatt is 1000 watts, always.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between direct current and alternating current?
prompts.answer: Direct current flows in one direction only; alternating current changes direction regularly.

prompts.prompt: What do d.c. and a.c. look like on a CRO screen?
prompts.answer: d.c.: a flat line on one side of zero. a.c.: a wave crossing the zero line.

prompts.prompt: Give the colour and the job of the live wire.
prompts.answer: Brown. It brings the supply into the appliance, through the fuse.

prompts.prompt: Give the colours of the neutral wire and the earth wire.
prompts.answer: Neutral is blue; earth is green and yellow.

prompts.prompt: Why is a switch always fitted in the live wire?
prompts.answer: So switching off cuts the appliance off from the live supply, and it cannot give a shock.

prompts.prompt: How does a fuse protect an appliance if a fault develops?
prompts.answer: The current becomes too high, the fuse wire melts, and the circuit is broken, so the current stops.

prompts.prompt: Why does a double-insulated appliance need no earth wire?
prompts.answer: Its case is plastic, so the outside can never become live.

prompts.prompt: How do you choose the fuse for an appliance on the 230 V mains?
prompts.answer: Work out I = P ÷ V, then take the smallest of 3 A, 5 A and 13 A above that current.

prompts.prompt: Which two parts of a plug work together to protect the user?
prompts.answer: The fuse and the earth wire.
